Mother Aldith wipes her hands on her apron, takes the note between two floury fingers, and reads it standing, with her lips moving. She reads it twice. Then she grunts.

"Edda Thorne's boy. She turned my first apprentice out of Millbrook with a cough and a loaf, and the girl's still the best midwife on the river. I'd know that hand of prayer anywhere." She squints at you. "You've her patience, I'd wager, and none of her sense, spending your slots on every crooked back in the valley."

She taps the note. "A dyer's girl of twelve who sweeps a chapel nobody asked her to sweep. That's the right sort, or the worst sort, and I'll know which in a week. Maud Marrow vouches for her?" Her mouth twitches. "I owe that woman a blanket and a favour. Send her down when the weather holds, with Maud for company and a month's trial, and I'll not promise more. I've had three apprentices and two stayed. Don't tell her I said yes before she's scrubbed a floor."

On Tobin, she is brisker. "A crushed ankle's no use waiting. Have Ansel bring him on a litter by nine, and I'll set it with my own hands. I'll want you there to hold the boy and say your hum, if you've a hum. Children set quieter with one." She jerks her chin. "And your dyer with the hip. Let him come, or not. A hip that's healed wrong must be re-broken to set right, and I won't do it to a man who's not ready for the pain. I'll tell you that plain, so you tell him plain."

She turns back to her dough. "Well? You've got to nine o'clock. Sit if you want to be useful, or go and fetch the boy."

Mother Aldith wipes her hands on her apron, takes the note, and reads it at arm's length with her lips moving. She snorts at the second line.

"Edda's boy. I heard she'd died. Good woman, hands like iron, never charged a widow a copper." She folds the note into her apron. "The ankle, yes. Bring the lad, or I'll come to him. A crushed ankle won't wait, and I'll set it before the swelling goes hard. Tell Ansel to have the boy fed and a strong dose of poppy in him by noon. I'll be there at the first bell."

Perrin Gale is a different matter. "A hip that healed wrong a month back? I can break it and set it again, but the old fool must want it. I'll not drag a man from his vats. If he comes, I'll see him. Tell him Aldith says it's the pain you remember, not the setting."

She puts your note on the shelf and tilts her head at you. "And your dyer's girl. A letter's a letter. I've had three prentices and two stayed, and I took the third on paper. She cried at the first bone. No. If the child wants it, she can walk here herself with Maud Marrow, who owes me a blanket, and I'll look at her hands and her stomach before I say a word. A month's trial I'll honour if she's fit. I'll not promise more."

It's not a refusal, and she isn't unkind. She goes back to the flour, and over her shoulder she says, "You've two prayers left, I'd guess, if you've sense. You'll want them today."

It's about twenty to seven on Day 6. You have 800 XP, 100 short of level 3, and the spells you prepared are all still ready. Tobin's bone will be set by noon. Perrin and Wren are both a journey away, and the bridge was quiet. The road beyond Stonebridge is open, but there may be more ghouls under the Drowned Stair.

input.add_to_description: Day 6 morning: Brannoc fumbled his pitch (Persuasion natural 1); she bristled at being told her business. She will see Tobin today (never turns the poor away), will not take Wren on a letter from a stranger, and says the girl must come herself and show her hands. entries.text:
You start well and go wrong in the middle. You name Edda, and then the boy, and the hip, and the girl, and Maud, and the parents, and the trial, all in one breath and in the order that suits you. You even hold out the note with the same hand that is still gesturing. Mother Aldith keeps kneading and doesn't look up until you're done.

"Two matters," she says. "You've given me five. And you've told me my business as if I'd lost the way to it." She wipes her hands on her apron, takes the note between two floury fingers and reads it in three breaths. "Edda's boy. She talked like a petition, too."

The mention of Maud earns you a grunt. It earns you nothing more.

"Tobin first. I don't turn a child from my door, and I'll not make him wait on your manners. Have Ansel's apprentice carry him here on a litter. I'll see to the ankle before noon, and I'll tell you now it'll be a bad week for him." She taps the note against the table. "The girl, no. I don't take prentices on a paper from a stranger. If she wants it, she walks here on her own feet, shows me her hands, and sits through a day of my temper. If she lasts, we talk. As for your dyer, a hip healed wrong is a month of work and a week of misery, and I'll not promise it for a man I've never seen. He can come, or not."

She turns back to the flour, and her voice softens by a hair. "Your note was well written, though. Put your name to the next one properly. I'd have said yes to Maud's stitches before I said yes to yours, and she knows it."

It's about twenty to seven on Day 6. Tobin can be carried over within the hour, and Aldith says she'll tend him and allow you to stay if you want to learn something. You've two 1st-level slots and full hit points. You're 100 XP short of level 3. The road home is open, and there's the bridge, Hodd, and whatever lies under the second arch.

"Good morning, Mother Aldith. I'm Brannoc Ashdown, Edda Thorne's foster-son, and I've come with two matters. A boy named Tobin has a crushed ankle at Brother Ansel's hospice, and a dyer in Greywater, Perrin Gale, has a hip that healed crooked after a fall from a rack."

I hold out the note. "This is also from me, for a dyer's daughter named Wren, twelve, who sweeps the chapel there and wants to learn the work. Maud Marrow vouches for her, and her parents have agreed to a month's trial. Will you read it, and will you see Tobin today?"

input.add_to_description: Day 6 morning: agreed to see Tobin that day, to look at Perrin Gale's hip if he comes to Stonebridge, and to meet Wren for a trial visit with Maud Marrow. Knew Edda Thorne by name. Wants Wren to be able to count breaths and keep a wound clean before she arrives.

entries.text:
Mother Aldith doesn't stop kneading. She jerks her chin at the note and says, "Read it to me. My hands are floury." You read the two lines aloud.

She grunts at the first line, and at the second she stops. "Maud Marrow's put her name to it, has she? That woman owes me two blankets and a lie about her brother's wool." She wipes her hands on her apron, takes the leaf, and reads it herself, lips moving. Persuasion (16): when she looks up, the scowl has not gone, but it has changed. "A dyer's girl who sweeps a dead priest's chapel for nothing. Edda took in strays too, and the best ones stayed." She tucks the note in her apron. "A month's trial, with Maud to chaperone. Send her in spring if the weather's foul. I'll not have a child on the road in mud. Tell her to learn her breaths and her bandages first. If she can't keep a wound clean, I can't use her."

Tobin she'll see today. "Send the boy on his litter. I'll have the table ready by noon. Crushed ankles want setting before the swelling sets hard." For Perrin, she is blunt. "Hips set crooked a month are a bad business. Tell him to come, and tell him I'll break it if I must and he'll hate me for it. Better hated than lame." She names a price, two silver, and says it can be paid in kind if he can't manage it.

She sizes you up once more. "You've a good face for the sick. A bad one for the rest. Don't spend yourself, boy. It's a long road for a cleric with no one behind him." Then she turns back to the dough as if you were already gone.

It's a quarter to seven on Day 6. You have two 1st-level slots, Channel Divinity, and 800 XP, 100 short of level 3. The hospice is waiting, Tobin will be carried here by noon, and the bridge is quiet. You may also take the valley road further, or stay in Stonebridge awhile and see whether the second arch is truly done.

input.add_to_description: Day 14 4:30 PM: Brannoc, Wick Hale and Gorm scouted from a skiff to the south tip. Jory's skiff is drawn up on the mud, empty. Brannoc's Perception 7 missed the finer detail: a trail of crushed reeds leads from the skiff around the mound's flank toward the west gap, Jory's dropped eel-spear lies in the mud, and one Wick-fire has begun to drift slowly toward the south tip.

entries.text:
Wick poles the skiff out over the dark water with long, steady strokes, and Gorm sits in the bow with a reed-knife across his knees. Nobody talks. The mist closes behind you until the landing is gone, and the Isle rises ahead out of the grey, a low hump ringed with dead-looking reeds. The air gets colder as you come in. You carry the rope, the hooded lantern, and a few flasks, and Shield of Faith waits ready on your tongue.

At half past four, forty yards off the south tip, you lay the skiff to and look.

Perception (7): you see only what is plain. Jory's skiff is there, drawn up on the mud in the cut reeds, empty, its painter tied to a stake. There's no sign of anyone beside it. You can't make out more than that through the mist and the cold glare of the water. If there are tracks, a dropped tool, or anything else on the mud, you haven't picked it out.

The Wick-fires hang over the west side as before, three pale glows. You watch them a long minute, and as you watch, you think one has shifted a little to the south. Wick has seen it too. He says in a low voice, "That one's moved. That wasn't there before."

It's half past four on Day 14, and you said nobody lands after half past four. The skiff drifts at the edge of the reeds. You have four 1st-level slots, no 2nd-level slots, and Channel Divinity. The light is going, and the glow is slowly coming this way.

input.add_to_description: Day 14 ~4:35 PM: From the water Brannoc saw Jory's skiff drawn up empty on the mud at the south tip, painter coiled neatly, bow-mark fresh. Brannoc missed (Perception 11) the second set of prints, bare and barefoot, leading from the skiff toward the west gap. Wick Hale saw the nearest Wick-fire slide a pace toward the skiff when they drifted in; they turned back as Brannoc had said. Jory's lantern is not in the skiff.

entries.text:
Yes. Wick poles you out through narrow channels between walls of reed, the mist closing behind, and Gorm sits in the bow with a spear across his knees. Nobody speaks. The skiff is cold, and the water is black and still. After forty minutes the south tip of the Isle rises out of the mist.

Jory came here, and he landed. The cut reeds lie in a raw swathe above the shore, and beyond them the mound's grass rises grey-green into the mist. You don't spot anything else, though you may well be missing it in the poor light.

Then Wick breathes a word through his teeth and stops poling. The nearest of the pale lights over the west side has slid a pace toward you across the water, slow and silent, and hangs there. The reeds under it have gone grey. Your skiff is thirty paces off the shore. It is twenty-five minutes to five, and you said you'd turn at the first sign of movement, so you do. Wick backs the skiff round with a long steady pull, and none of you speak until the Isle is a smear in the mist.

You reach the landing a little after a quarter past five. Ode is there waiting, and she sees your face and asks nothing. You tell her about the skiff. Her jaw tightens, and she says only, "He landed, then." Dusk is a quarter-hour away, and the village is cooking by the fires. In the Long House the sick sleep.

You have four 1st-level slots, no 2nd-level slots, and Channel Divinity. You can't finish another long rest before half past three tomorrow afternoon. The Wick-fires are patient. Jory has been on the Isle five days.

I'll bring the rope, the hooded lantern, and a few flasks of oil, and keep Shield of Faith ready. I'll watch the bow-mark and the cut reeds for Jory's skiff or any sign of him. DM: can I see from the water whether Jory's skiff is still tied up at the south tip?

input.add_to_description: Day 14 ~4:40 PM: Scouted from the skiff (Wick Hale poling, Gorm Hale). Jory's skiff is beached on the south-tip mud, its painter looped over a stump, empty; his cold lantern and a dropped eel-spear lie in the cut reeds; bootprints lead up the slope toward the west, and a second set of prints beside them: bare, long, narrow feet, wet and fresh. The Wick-fires drifted slowly toward the skiff as it neared and hung at the reed edge, watching.

entries.text:
You take the rope, the hooded lantern, and a few flasks, and Ode's skiff slips out from the staithe with Wick at the pole and Gorm in the bow. Water chuckles under the hull, and the reeds close in on both sides, hissing, then fall behind. The mist thickens as you go. You say little. It takes about three-quarters of an hour of steady poling. The Isle rises slowly out of the grey, reed-ringed and low, and the Wick-fires hang in the haze at its west end.

At a quarter to five you glide in close to the south tip. Perception (13), just enough: a skiff lies pulled up on the mud, its painter looped around a stump. It is empty. A cold lantern lies in the cut reeds beside it, and a dropped eel-spear. Bootprints lead up the slope toward the west, a man's boots, long-striding then stumbling. And beside them, over them in places, is a second set of prints. They are bare, long, and narrow, wet and fresh in the mud, not half a day old.

As the skiff nears, the three Wick-fires drift. Slowly, not like marsh-gas, they slide along the reed-edge toward you and hang a stone's throw off, pale and still. Nothing else moves. Gorm's knuckles are white on the gunwale. Wick says low, "Those are watching us, priest."

It's twenty to five on Day 14. The sun is lowering, and dusk is about forty-five minutes off. Jory's skiff is here, and the prints say he walked to the west door, and something followed him, or met him. You have four 1st-level slots, no 2nd-level slots, and Channel Divinity. You said nobody lands after half past four, and nobody goes near the west door.

sheet.name: Brannoc Ashdown
sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.

features: Divine Domain: Choose one domain related to your deity, such as Life. Each domain is detailed at the end of the class description, and each one provides examples of gods associated with it. Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Channel Divinity (1/rest): At 2nd level, you gain the ability to channel divine energy directly from your deity, using that energy to fuel magical effects. You start with two such effects: Turn Undead and an effect determined by your domain. Some domains grant you additional effects as you advance in levels, as noted in the domain description. When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 3: 15 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

input.add_to_description: Day 14 4:35 PM: Brannoc's natural 20 Perception from the water: Jory's skiff is drawn up on the south-tip mud, rope neatly coiled, lantern gone. Faint voice from a crack at the mound's south flank calling 'Aunt? Anyone?': Jory is alive, in the mound. entries.text:
You gather the rope, the hooded lantern, and six flasks. Wick poles the skiff, and Gorm sits in the bow with an eel-spear across his knees. The water is black and still, the mist low, and the reeds close in on both sides until the channel is a green corridor with a grey sky above it. Nobody talks. The only sound is the pole in the mud.

At twenty-five to five you come in sight of the south tip, thirty paces off. Perception (20, a natural 20): the whole picture comes clear to you at once.

Jory's skiff is there, drawn up neatly on the mud, the rope coiled on the thwart, but his lantern is gone. A track of boot-prints leads up the bank and into a dark crack at the mound's south flank, half hidden by grass. And from that crack, faint and cracked, a voice. "Aunt? Anyone? Please." He's alive.

And you see what the cutters broke. Round the whole Isle, half sunk in the mud, runs a ring of old stones, each carved with a deep circle. The reeds grew over them, thick as a wall, and held them. On the south tip the cutters hacked the reeds back and tore two of the stones from their places. The ring is broken there, a gap of ten paces. The fallen standing stone at the west end is carved the same way. It looks like a ward, and the cutters cut its cover and opened it. Behind it, to the west, the three Wick-fires hang. They have not moved.

It's twenty-five to five on Day 14. Dusk is about an hour off. You have four 1st-level slots and no 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, six flasks, rope, and Gorm and Wick in the skiff. You said nobody lands after half past four. The voice comes again, weaker.
